seoDescription: Learn how to implement robust user authentication in your Django projects by leveraging built-in features for login and logout. This tutorial guides you through creating login templates, integrating Django's `contrib.auth` URLs, and customizing redirects after login or logout. Discover how to restrict access to specific pages for authenticated users using the `user.is_authenticated` attribute in your templates and views, and see how to access the current user object to build more secure applications.

chapters.title: Introduction to User Authentication
chapters.description: This chapter introduces the video's topic: implementing login, logout, and restricting page access for authenticated users in Django.

chapters.title: Integrating Django's Built-in Auth URLs
chapters.description: Learn how to use Django's built-in authentication application by including its URL patterns in your project's main urls.py file.

chapters.title: Creating the Login Template
chapters.description: This chapter walks through creating the required directory structure and the login.html template that Django's auth views expect.

chapters.title: Configuring Login Redirects
chapters.description: Learn how to override Django's default post-login redirect destination by setting the LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL in your settings.py file.

chapters.title: Checking Authentication with `user.is_authenticated`
chapters.description: This chapter demonstrates how to use the user.is_authenticated attribute in templates to conditionally render content for logged-in users.

chapters.title: Logout Redirects and Accessing User in Views
chapters.description: Learn how to set a custom redirect URL for logging out and how to access the current user object from within a Django view.

chapters.title: Conclusion and Next Steps
chapters.description: This chapter concludes the tutorial, summarizes what was covered, and provides a preview of the next video on custom user models.

summary:
## Key Concepts for Django User Authentication This document summarizes the core steps for implementing login, logout, and user authentication in a Django application. ### 1. Activating Django's Auth URLs Django provides a built-in set of views and URLs for handling common authentication tasks. - To use them, include the `django.contrib.auth.urls` in your project's main `urls.py` file. ```python # my_site/urls.py from django.urls import path, include urlpatterns = [ # ... your other urls path('', include('django.contrib.auth.urls')), ] ``` ### 2. Creating Authentication Templates Django's authentication views automatically look for templates in a specific location. > [!NOTE] > You must create a `registration` folder inside one of your app's `templates` directories. The login template must be named `login.html`. > Example path: `my_app/templates/registration/login.html` - The **login.html** template should contain a form that posts to the login view. The view passes a `form` object to the template context automatically. ```html {% extends 'main/base.html' %} {% load crispy_forms_tags %} {% block content %}
{% csrf_token %} {{ form|crispy }}

Don't have an account? Create one here.

{% endblock %} ``` ### 3. Configuring Redirects After a successful login or logout, Django needs to know where to send the user. > [!IMPORTANT] > By default, Django redirects to `/accounts/profile/` after login. If this route doesn't exist, you'll get a 404 error. Configure these settings in your `settings.py` file. - **`LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL`**: Specifies the path to redirect to after a successful login. `'/`' is a common choice for the homepage. - **`LOGOUT_REDIRECT_URL`**: Specifies the path to redirect to after logging out. This can also be set to the homepage or a dedicated "Logged Out" page. ```python # settings.py LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL = '/' LOGOUT_REDIRECT_URL = '/' ``` ### 4. Checking Authentication Status You can check if the current user is logged in within both templates and views. - **In Templates**: The `user` object is available in the template context. Use the **`user.is_authenticated`** boolean attribute to conditionally display content. ```html {% if user.is_authenticated %}

Welcome, {{ user.username }}!

Logout {% else %}

You are not logged in.

Login {% endif %} ``` - **In Views**: The `request` object contains the current `user`. > [!TIP] > The video mentions `response.user`, but the correct way to access the user in a view is through the `request` object: **`request.user`**. The `request.user` object will be an instance of the `User` model if logged in, or an `AnonymousUser` object if not. ```python # views.py def my_view(request): if request.user.is_authenticated: # Do something for logged in users pass # ... ```
